rewrite.question: Two rules in the same stylesheet, with no layers and no `!important`, have identical specificity and set the same property. What decides which one applies?

The one written last
The one with the shorter selector

rewrite.explanation: When origin, layer, importance and specificity all tie, the last declaration in source order wins. rationale: Shorthand verified on MDN and the stretch behaviour in CSS 2.2 §10.3.7/§10.6.4 (width/height auto with both edges set → solve for the size). Options balanced.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/inset — "corresponds to the top, right, bottom, and/or left properties"; "have no effect on non-positioned elements"

https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS22/visudet.html — §10.3.7 "'width' is 'auto', 'left' and 'right' are not 'auto', then solve for 'width'"; §10.6.4 "'height' is 'auto', 'top' and 'bottom' are not 'auto', then … solve for 'height'"

objective: Escape a clipping ancestor structurally: render the dropdown outside it (portal) or in the top layer via popover/dialog.
defects: hint is the generic fallback
key is markedly longer than the distractors (automated flag confirmed); "Removing the parent's padding" is a throwaway
no support statement for the top-layer route: MDN marks the Popover API Baseline "Newly available" since January 2025

options: Give the dropdown a larger `z-index` than the ancestor
Render it outside the clipping ancestor: a portal, or the top layer via `popover`
Remove the padding from the clipping ancestor
Set `overflow: visible` on the dropdown itself
rewrite.hint: The clip is applied by an ancestor to everything inside it. Ask which option changes where the dropdown is, rather than how it is painted.
rewrite.explanation: Clipping is decided by the ancestor, so the fix is to not be inside it: render the dropdown elsewhere in the tree (a portal) or put it in the top layer with the `popover` attribute or a `<dialog>`, which paints above everything without depending on stacking order or ancestors' overflow. A z-index never overrides clipping, `overflow: visible` on the child does not undo the parent's clip, and padding is unrelated. Popover has been available in all major browsers since January 2025.

rationale: Key verified: the top layer sits above all other layers and is the documented home of popover and modal dialog; overflow clipping is per ancestor. The rewrite dates the support claim and replaces the throwaway distractor.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Top_layer — "a specific layer that spans the entire width and height of the viewport and sits on top of all other layers displayed in a web document"; contains fullscreen elements, modal <dialog>, popovers shown via showPopover()
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Popover_API — Baseline 2025 "Newly available … Since January 2025, this feature works across the latest devices and browser versions"
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/overflow — hidden clips at the element's padding box

objective: Contrast custom properties (runtime values that cascade, inherit and can be scripted) with preprocessor variables (compiled away).
defects: hint is the generic fallback
key is markedly longer than the distractors (automated flag confirmed)

options: Smaller stylesheets after the build step
A live value in the browser that cascades, inherits and can change per element
Support in browsers older than the preprocessor
Type checking of the value at build time
rewrite.hint: Ask what is left of each kind of variable once the browser receives the stylesheet.
rewrite.explanation: A preprocessor variable is substituted at build time and is gone before the browser sees the file. A custom property is live: it participates in the cascade, inherits down the tree, can be redefined on any element and read or set from JavaScript — which is what makes theming by scope possible at all. It does not shrink files, older browsers handle preprocessor output better, and no CSS variable is type checked.

rationale: Key verified (inherited: yes; participate in the cascade; runtime access). Options balanced to comparable length.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/--* — "scoped to the element(s) they are declared on, and participate in the cascade"; Inherited: yes; can be redefined on a subtree and read/set via the CSSOM

objective: Apply custom-property inheritance: redefine the token on the component's element to reskin its subtree.
defects: hint is the generic fallback

rewrite.hint: The component's rules read the token, not the colour. Ask where a new value has to be declared for everything inside the component to pick it up.
rewrite.explanation: Custom properties inherit, so redefining the accent token on the component's own element reskins everything under it that reads the token — no rule inside the component changes. That is the whole design: components read the token and never the value. `!important` overrides fight the cascade rule by rule, duplicated styles drift apart, and a second stylesheet still has to override each declaration.

rationale: Key verified by MDN's own subtree-override example (#container { --first-color: … }). The four options are the four real approaches. Hint only.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/--* — Inherited: yes; example overriding `--first-color` on `#container` for its subtree

objective: Understand that a utility-class approach flattens specificity so conflicts are decided by which classes are applied (and stylesheet order), not selector weight.
defects: hint is the generic fallback
key is a 20-word sentence against one- to three-word distractors ("Nothing", "It disables the cascade") — automated flag confirmed

"conflicts are resolved by which class is applied" is imprecise: when two applied utilities set the same property, the later one in the generated stylesheet wins, not the later one in the class attribute

options: Nothing: the cascade is bypassed entirely
Every rule has the same low specificity, so which class is applied decides
Inheritance is switched off for utility-styled elements
Specificity is raised so each utility always wins
rewrite.hint: Write out the specificity of `.p-4` and `.mt-2`. Ask what is left for the cascade to decide when every rule in the sheet looks like that.
rewrite.explanation: Every utility is a single class selector at 0-1-0, so nothing in the sheet outranks anything else: the cascade is not gone, it simply never has a specificity contest to run. You control the result by choosing which classes go on the element, and when two applied utilities set the same property, the later one in the generated stylesheet wins. Inheritance and the box model are untouched underneath, and no utility raises specificity.

rationale: The underlying cascade fact is verifiable (single-class selectors tie at 0-1-0 and fall through to source order) and is a reasonable architecture lesson for level 6, but learning value is modest and the original options are badly unbalanced. Passes both gates after rewrite at quality 3.
evidence: node: rm-css-44 utility class .p-4 = 0,1,0 ; .mt-2 = 0,1,0 -> equal, order decides
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Specificity — class selectors add 0-1-0; equal specificity → "The last declared selector wins"

objective: Explain why removing the focus outline harms keyboard users and how :focus-visible restores an indicator.
defects: hint is the generic fallback

rewrite.hint: Think about who navigates with Tab rather than a pointer, and what changes for them when the outline goes.
rewrite.explanation: The focus ring is how someone who is not using a mouse knows what Enter will activate; `outline: none` on `:focus` removes that with nothing in its place, and keyboard navigation becomes guesswork for sighted users. If the default ring clashes with the design, replace it with a visible one — `:focus-visible` shows it for keyboard use and not for mouse clicks. The declaration is valid CSS, and it changes neither layout nor event handlers.

rationale: Verified against MDN's accessibility note (removing focus styles makes keyboard navigation inaccessible for sighted users) and the :focus-visible heuristic. Hint only.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/:focus-visible — "Removing focus styles makes keyboard navigation inaccessible for sighted users"; "focus styles are always required when users are navigating the page with the keyboard"; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.11 requires the indicator to be at least 3:1

objective: Apply WCAG 1.4.1: never convey status by colour alone; add a word, icon or shape.
defects: hint is the generic fallback
explanation does not name the criterion (WCAG 1.4.1) or mention screen readers

rewrite.hint: Imagine the same screen in greyscale, or read aloud. Ask what still tells the user that something went wrong.
rewrite.explanation: Colour alone excludes anyone who cannot distinguish it, disappears in high-contrast modes and on poor screens, and is invisible to a screen reader; WCAG 1.4.1 says colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information. The word "Error" or an icon beside the red does the work for everyone. Font size, z-index and transitions change nothing about whether the meaning is perceivable.

rationale: Verified against the WCAG 2.2 Understanding document for 1.4.1; the item also matches this product's own non-colour-status rule. Hint only.
evidence: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html — SC 1.4.1: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element"; text labels, icons and patterns as additional cues

objective: Apply prefers-reduced-motion: remove movement (vestibular triggers) while keeping non-motion feedback such as a fade.
defects: hint is the generic fallback

"What should … do" asks for a judgement without a criterion, so "Remove both" is a defensible conservative choice; the question must ask for the change that respects the setting without losing feedback
the two effects are not tied to properties (`transform` vs `opacity`), which is what makes the distinction testable

rewrite.question: A card lifts (`transform`) and fades in (`opacity`) when it appears. Inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, which change respects the setting without losing the feedback?
options: Leave both as they are — it is only a preference
Remove the movement and keep the fade
Remove both the movement and the fade
Make both faster so they finish sooner
rewrite.hint: The setting is about motion, not about change. Ask which of the two effects moves anything across the screen.
rewrite.explanation: The preference exists mainly for vestibular discomfort, which movement — scaling, sliding, panning — causes and an opacity change does not, so freezing the transform is the change that matters. Removing the fade too loses the feedback for no benefit, ignoring the setting is what the media query is there to prevent, and faster motion is still motion.

rationale: MDN's own example makes exactly this distinction (replace a scale animation with an opacity dissolve), so the key is the documented practice; the rewrite states the criterion so "remove both" is no longer defensible.
evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion — "minimize the amount of non-essential motion"; "Animations such as scaling or panning large objects can be vestibular motion triggers"; example replaces a transform: scale() pulse with an opacity dissolve under (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)

objective: Attribute zoom breakage to fixed pixel heights on text containers (WCAG 1.4.4 Resize text, 1.4.10 Reflow).
defects: hint is the generic fallback
explanation does not name the criteria (1.4.4 at 200%, 1.4.10 reflow)

rewrite.hint: Zoom enlarges the text. Ask which of the four choices stops the box around that text from growing with it.
rewrite.explanation: Zooming makes the text larger and a fixed `height` does not follow, so the content overflows or is clipped — WCAG 1.4.4 requires text to resize to 200% without loss of content, and 1.4.10 requires reflow without two-dimensional scrolling. Sizing from the content with `min-height` survives it. `rem` spacing scales with the text, Grid and custom properties are neutral, and zoom is the cheapest accessibility test there is.

rationale: Verified against WCAG 2.2 Understanding documents: 1.4.4 names clipped/truncated text at 200% as the failure and requires text containers to resize with the text. Hint only.
evidence: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/resize-text.html — SC 1.4.4 "Text can be resized without assistive technology up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality"; failure when resizing "causes the text, image or controls to be clipped, truncated or obscured"; "text containers resize when the text resizes"
https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow.html — SC 1.4.10: content presented without loss of information and without two-dimensional scrolling at 320 CSS px width
